title_en: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed, as New York braces for huge storm
content_en:
The unprecedented move comes amid concerns about how the event’s massive balloons would fare during the intense winds predicted.
A Buzz Lightyear balloon rests under protective netting during the inflation on Wednesday for Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York. Photo: AFP
Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade will also be a first: organisers made an unprecedented decision to postpone the event to Saturday because of bad weather.
The annual parade, originally scheduled for Thursday, has been moved “out of an abundance of caution” and following consultation with city officials about the severe weather, Macy’s said in a statement on Wednesday.
“Our team is now working through the complex operational logistics required to bring the Parade to life on Saturday, and we will share additional details as they are finalised,” the company said.
The postponement came as New York is set to get slammed by a storm bringing intense winds and rain to the region, which had raised worries about how the parade’s massive balloons would fare while floating through the windswept canyons between Manhattan’s skyscrapers and over throngs of spectators lining the streets below.
The National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning and a coastal flood warning for Thursday into Friday.
Workers inflate a Spider-Man balloon on Wednesday for the 100th Annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York. Photo: EPA
The city’s emergency management agency has been warning residents about the possible storm, with officials banning empty articulated lorries from bridges on Thursday morning because of the wind.
NBC, which airs the parade, said it will instead broadcast a rerun of the 2025 edition Thursday. It was not immediately clear whether the event’s expansive line-up of performers would also shift to the new date.
The parade’s iconic balloons were well on the way to being inflated when the postponement was announced. Macy’s representatives had repeatedly put off interviews on-site, raising eyebrows among the city’s news media ahead of the official postponement.
A spokesman for the retail giant said it was the first time the event has been postponed. It was cancelled for three years – in 1942, 1943 and 1944 – during World War II, the spokesman said.
Workers inflate a Donkey balloon on Wednesday before the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York. Photo: EPA
The city has long had measures in place that dictate whether to lower the balloons or cancel their flights entirely if the wind gets too strong, due to concerns that strong winds can knock them off course and into spectators along the parade route.
The rules were put in place after high winds sent a balloon careering into a metal pole during the 1997 parade, leaving a woman in a coma.
Bad weather in the past has caused balloons to be flown a bit lower than usual, with each inflatable character having a distinct risk profile that includes its size and weight and optimal altitudes for differing wind speeds.
The rescheduled parade will kick off at 8.30am on Saturday, Macy’s said in a statement.
By Associated Press

title_en: US trading partners’ patience wears thin as Trump slaps on new tariffs
content_en:
Resignation and frustration reign as predictable US president announces fresh tariffs on 14 major economies, including China.
US President Donald Trump announces worldwide tariffs on April 2, 2025. Photo: Getty Images/TNS
Major US trading partners and companies on the economic front lines decried US President Donald Trump’s latest tariff salvo on Wednesday, even as they expressed resignation, as his playbook has become more predictable and better telegraphed with repeated use.
This followed the White House’s proposal of fresh tariffs a few hours earlier on 14 major economies, including China, a week after Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.
The new levies, subject to a public comment period, would lift total duties on targeted economies from 15 to 20 per cent. This comes as the transactional US president looks for alternatives after the US Supreme Court struck down his broad-based “emergency” tariffs in February.
“Partners have been waiting for this shoe to drop for some time,” said Wendy Cutler, senior vice-president with the Asia Society Policy Institute. “Many have publicly and privately pushed back in recent months, stressing that they are being wrongly accused of producing too much in selected sectors.”
The latest tariff announcement tied to excess industrial capacity follows other levies outlined in July tied to forced labour.
[embedded media]
This steady drumbeat of trade barriers will only increase incentives among economies worldwide to shift their supply chains away from US shores. “Make no mistake. These tariffs will continue to accelerate diversification efforts,” added Cutler, a former senior US trade negotiator.
Trading partners from Beijing to Brussels expressed their displeasure on Wednesday even as they pushed back on the overproduction rationale.
“Tariff wars and trade wars serve no one’s interests,” said Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun. “The so-called issue of overcapacity is a false proposition, and China opposes using it as a pretext for political manipulation.”
“India does not have structural excess capacity in any sector,” the country’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry said, while Bernd Lange, head of the European Union Parliament’s trade committee, called such charges “absurd”.
“If Washington breaches its commitments, the EU must act swiftly,” Lange added. “It has the legal means to do so.”
South Korea, like many countries, said it was studying Wednesday’s US Trade Representative announcement, adding in a statement that an ultimate rate of 15 per cent would be a “good outcome”, while noting that Washington has left open the possibility of raising it to 25 per cent “depending on the outcome of future consultations”.
The tone from many countries after the announcement was relatively muted, however, analysts said. The Supreme Court slapdown of his use of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act has blunted his ability to apply punitive trade measures at will, they said.
And under the various workarounds the self-declared “tariff man” has reached for since then, including Section 301, 232, 122 and 338 trade provisions, most involve lead time, laid-out processes and hearings that reduce the impact and make planning easier.
This stands in sharp contrast to the global shock when his 2025 “Liberation Day” onslaught was announced.
US small business owners unhappy with latest tariff proposal
That does not mean, however, that small business owners welcome his latest move, as they cited its impact on input costs and prices for consumers already grappling with a US affordability crisis.
“Customers can’t afford more price increases, but small businesses can’t afford to absorb tariffs on top [of] tariffs either,” said Dan Anthony, executive director of “We Pay the Tariffs”, a coalition of small businesses.
“As if their unpopularity wasn’t bad enough, the tariffs also have failed to achieve any of the administration’s stated objectives,” he added.
Experts widely viewed elevated tariffs, combined with higher energy prices triggered by the conflict in Iran, as key drivers of Republican setbacks in the recent US midterm elections – a political cost that has done little to deter the White House from pressing ahead with fresh import duties.
[embedded media]
“Any additional tariffs will further exacerbate the situation and put many restaurants in the USA on the precipice of failure,” said Fred Mortati, the owner of Orlando Food Sales, a New Jersey-based food importer and distributor.
“We are begging Congress to listen to its constituents and not allow further price increases by way of additional tariffs.”
Figures released on Wednesday showed the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index increased 0.3 per cent in October from a month earlier, lifting the annual inflation rate to 3.8 per cent.
Democrats’ growing clout after Trump’s party was drubbed in the midterms has also led to more pushback.
Chuck Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, said Wednesday that the president’s actions continue to alienate allies while “passing the costs onto American families”.
“Donald Trump never learns,” he wrote on social media, adding that the “bad actor is China” even as the administration has failed to address the role of the Asian giant.
“Change is coming in January,” Schumer promised.
The Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus (CAPAC) also said Trump’s “reckless trade wars” have made life costlier for Asian-American, Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders, as many of them rely on imports that cannot be produced domestically.
The caucus vowed to use the incoming Democratic majority to roll back the duties.
“Next year, CAPAC members will reclaim Congress’s constitutional authority under Article I to regulate trade and work to end these costly tariffs once and for all,” said Representative Grace Meng, the New York Democrat who chairs the caucus.
[embedded media]
Congress has the power under the Constitution to levy taxes and tariffs and to regulate foreign commerce, authority that lawmakers have largely delegated to the executive branch over the decades.
But analysts said China has concluded that it is competitive enough to weather 20 per cent tariffs, especially if other countries face similar US restrictions, and will continue to back the trade truce despite Trump’s weakened political stature.
“Beijing will prioritise stability over exploiting Trump’s weakened position, responding proportionately to US restrictions, while mutual vulnerabilities will deter severe escalation,” said Dominic Chiu, senior analyst with the Eurasia Group, in a report.
A September study by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that for every percentage point increase in average tariffs, consumer goods prices rose by about a quarter of a per cent after one year.
Analysis shows 90 per cent of 2025 tariffs paid by US producers, consumers
The analysis also showed that nearly 90 per cent of the 2025 tariffs were paid by US producers and consumers, not the export country, as Trump has claimed.
While the new tariffs are unlikely to directly disrupt the fragile US-China truce, the move adds another layer of complexity to ongoing negotiations over extending the Busan agreement, which expires on January 10, 2027.
Under the deal signed in South Korea last year, Washington reduced tariffs on certain Chinese imports and suspended additional trade restrictions in return for a pause on China’s rare earth export controls and a pledge to resume US agricultural purchases.
Analysts said the timing of Wednesday’s tariff announcement – after the politically sensitive midterm elections and last week’s Trump-Xi meeting and three weeks before the G20 convenes in Miami – was hardly coincidental.
And it lets Trump keep much of what he relishes: leverage to make deals, to counter others’ leverage and to impose his will on smaller players.
“Of note, the US indicated that it retains the flexibility to raise these tariffs if ongoing bilateral talks fail or China does not live up to its commitments,” said Cutler.
“Clearly, the US is using these tariffs as leverage to secure expected shipments of critical minerals and rare earths, and further purchases of US agricultural goods.”
China on Tuesday extended its suspension of export restrictions on US-bound shipments of gallium, germanium and antimony until January 27, aligning the two-month reprieve with ongoing talks over extending the Busan agreement.
Both sides are also taking steps to implement the US-China Board of Trade, which oversees tariff-reduced trade in non-sensitive goods worth up to US$30 billion on each side.
By Mark Magnier, Nayan Seth, Finbarr Bermingham

title_en: US federal court blocks new Trump birthright citizenship executive order
content_en:
US judge on Wednesday blocked enforcement of US president’s second executive order after US Supreme Court rejected ‌his initial effort.
A protester holds a sign in support of birthright citizenship outside the US Supreme Court in Washington, in May 2025. Photo: AP
A federal judge on Wednesday blocked US President Donald Trump’s latest executive order aimed at restricting birthright citizenship, dealing another setback to his ongoing effort to redefine what it means to be born an American.
“Enough is enough,” said Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the American Civil Liberties Union’s Immigrants’ Rights Project. “The Supreme Court has twice rejected efforts to gut birthright citizenship, in 1898 and again earlier this year.
“Third time is not the charm, and the president needs to accept that birthright citizenship is the law of the land.”
Limiting birthright citizenship has been a cornerstone of Trump’s second-term agenda as part of his aggressive immigration agenda, and he has sought to curtail it in multiple ways since returning to office, including in a previous executive order the US Supreme Court struck down earlier this year.
Trump signed the initial executive order on his first day back in office in 2025.
US President Donald Trump signs an executive order on birthright citizenship in the Oval Office in January 2025. Photo: AP
That order directed federal agencies not to recognise the citizenship of children born in the US to parents who were undocumented or present on temporary visas.
The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 against him in Trump vs Barbara in June, holding that children born in the US to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present are citizens at birth under the 14th Amendment.
Following his Supreme Court loss, Trump issued another executive order in August that sought to expand the categories of children who the government says are not entitled to birthright citizenship.
Among those targeted were children whose parents worked for foreign governments or certain international organisations, as well as children born through commercial birth tourism and surrogacy arrangements.
In response, the American Civil Liberties Union and other advocacy groups filed a lawsuit, Nathan vs Trump, in September on behalf of those who would be subject to the new executive order, leading to Wednesday’s preliminary decision.
In his preliminary injunction on the second executive order on Wednesday, US District Judge Christopher Cooper in Washington said that “Barbara’s ink had scarcely dried when the President issued a second executive order”.
Cooper noted that the Supreme Court had already recognised that these children are US citizens.
“As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the president cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws,” wrote Cooper.
The judge also highlighted that the practice of birth tourism violates US law, “under which ‘obtaining US citizenship for a child’ is an impermissible basis for a tourist visa”.
Trump has often taken advantage of the courts’ slow pace to impose “facts on the ground”, even if there is a high likelihood his administration’s actions will be overruled.
In the months since the Supreme Court ruling, the Trump administration has increasingly focused on birth tourism, particularly cases involving Chinese nationals.
“I would like to congratulate President Xi and the Great Country of China on their massive Birthright Citizenship WIN! President DONALD J. TRUMP,” Trump wrote on social media after the Supreme Court verdict.
While birth tourism exists, available statistics indicate the practice is very rare.
Cooper is not the only judge to block the second executive order.
In September, US District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland issued a preliminary injunction at the request of immigrant rights advocates, noting that the president’s order was “almost certainly unconstitutional”.
By Lucy Quaggin

title_en: Colombia quiet as China says lawmakers’ Taiwan trip crossed its ‘first red line’
content_en:
Beijing’s embassy objects after senator dubbed Taipei’s envoy ‘ambassador’, but De la Espriella’s ministry does not comment on controversy.
Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung met with Colombian Senator Luis Perez in Taipei in September 2025 to strengthen bilateral cooperation and economic ties. Photo: CNA
A multiparty group of Colombian lawmakers visiting Taiwan has drawn a formal protest from China, while President Abelardo de la Espriella’s government has stayed silent for two days as of Wednesday, even as the pressure from Beijing has intensified.
China’s embassy in Bogota demanded on Monday that both the government and Congress “publicly reiterate” their commitment to the one-China principle and “immediately take effective measures to correct the error and eliminate the negative impact”.
It called Taiwan the “first insurmountable red line” in relations with Colombia, which switched diplomatic recognition from Taipei to Beijing in 1980.
Beijing’s sharpest complaint concerned the way one lawmaker addressed the head of the Taipei Commercial Office in Bogota, Taiwan’s unofficial mission in Colombia.
Senator German Rodriguez of the right-wing Salvacion Nacional movement called him “ambassador” in a video recorded before the trip and listed Taiwan among Colombia’s friendly “countries”, according to Colombian media.
[embedded media]
The embassy said the office was “merely an unofficial economic and trade body without any diplomatic status” and that the lawmakers had travelled “in an official capacity” despite “solemn representations and repeated dissuasion” from Beijing.
It also asked Bogota to halt all official exchanges with the Taiwanese authorities and accused Taipei of winning over foreign politicians “through money and deception”.
The Taipei office answered on social media that it rejected “claims that do not correspond to reality” and that Beijing had offered “no concrete evidence”.
Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed by law to supplying it with weapons.
The nine senators and representatives landed in Taipei on Monday and are due to leave on Friday. They belong to seven parties, from former president Gustavo Petro’s leftist Pacto Historico party to right-wing allies of the government, and all sit on the congressional committees for foreign affairs and trade.
As of Wednesday afternoon, neither De la Espriella nor Foreign Minister Omar Bula had said anything about the protest.
China is Colombia’s second-largest trading partner after the United States. When its top legislator Zhao Leji hosted lower house speaker Nicolas Barguil and a multiparty delegation in Beijing earlier this month, Barguil told him that Colombia “firmly supports” the one-China principle, according to Xinhua.
Third congressional trip to Taipei in 14 months
Colombian lawmakers have travelled to Taipei three times since September 2025, when a Taiwan friendship caucus led by Senator Jose Luis Perez met Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung.
Two months later, the chairs of the Senate and lower house foreign affairs committees told Lin they would push for Colombia to reopen an office on the island.
Petro was still president, and his foreign ministry disowned those remarks the next day, saying they “neither reflect nor commit” the country to any change in its official position. Petro then postponed a trip to Beijing planned for December and left office in August without having made it.
The former president started the latest row himself on Saturday, two days before the embassy’s statement, when he posted a photo of the delegation on social media and wrote that “one should not help divide a civilisation for the sake of tourism”.
Two Pacto Historico senators were on the trip, and one of them, Agmeth Escaf, answered Petro within hours.
“Both our country Colombia and our party, the Pacto Historico, recognise one China, and this visit by congressmen to Taiwan does not alter, question or seek to modify that position,” Escaf wrote.

Senator Mary Jurado posted her own defence on Sunday and called the trip “strictly parliamentary” work, “not a tourism trip”.

Bula has called China “the filth of the planet”, according to the Colombian news site La Silla Vacia, though he said after being named that he wanted a “pragmatic” relationship with Beijing.
Seven of Taiwan’s 12 remaining diplomatic allies are in Latin America and the Caribbean: Paraguay, Guatemala, Belize, Haiti, St Kitts and Nevis, St Lucia and St Vincent and the Grenadines.
Beijing sanctioned a Paraguayan and a Belizean minister in October over their countries’ ties with Taipei. Honduras cut ties with Taiwan in 2023, but Nasry Asfura won the presidency last year on a promise to restore them.

title_display: Colombia quiet as China says lawmakers’ Taiwan trip crossed its ‘first red line’

Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung met with Colombian Senator Luis Perez in Taipei in September 2025 to strengthen bilateral cooperation and economic ties. Photo: CNA
A multiparty group of Colombian lawmakers visiting Taiwan has drawn a formal protest from China, while President Abelardo de la Espriella’s government has stayed silent for two days as of Wednesday, even as the pressure from Beijing has intensified.
China’s embassy in Bogota demanded on Monday that both the government and Congress “publicly reiterate” their commitment to the one-China principle and “immediately take effective measures to correct the error and eliminate the negative impact”.
It called Taiwan the “first insurmountable red line” in relations with Colombia, which switched diplomatic recognition from Taipei to Beijing in 1980.
Beijing’s sharpest complaint concerned the way one lawmaker addressed the head of the Taipei Commercial Office in Bogota, Taiwan’s unofficial mission in Colombia.
Senator German Rodriguez of the right-wing Salvacion Nacional movement called him “ambassador” in a video recorded before the trip and listed Taiwan among Colombia’s friendly “countries”, according to Colombian media.
[embedded media]
The embassy said the office was “merely an unofficial economic and trade body without any diplomatic status” and that the lawmakers had travelled “in an official capacity” despite “solemn representations and repeated dissuasion” from Beijing.
It also asked Bogota to halt all official exchanges with the Taiwanese authorities and accused Taipei of winning over foreign politicians “through money and deception”.
The Taipei office answered on social media that it rejected “claims that do not correspond to reality” and that Beijing had offered “no concrete evidence”.
Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed by law to supplying it with weapons.
The nine senators and representatives landed in Taipei on Monday and are due to leave on Friday. They belong to seven parties, from former president Gustavo Petro’s leftist Pacto Historico party to right-wing allies of the government, and all sit on the congressional committees for foreign affairs and trade.
As of Wednesday afternoon, neither De la Espriella nor Foreign Minister Omar Bula had said anything about the protest.
China is Colombia’s second-largest trading partner after the United States. title_en: Massive blaze kills at least 30 in Cairo, Egypt, after fuel truck overturns
content_en:
39 ambulances were sent to the scene after a fire erupted in a densely populated section of the capital.
Damaged cars are seen as firefighters extinguish a fire involving a vehicle carrying petroleum products just outside Cairo, Egypt, on Wednesday. Photo: AP
A fire erupted in Egypt’s capital on Wednesday, killing at least 30 people, according to the health ministry, after a fuel truck reportedly overturned on a packed highway.
Footage shot by passers-by showed a massive blaze and huge clouds of smoke rising from the site in Cairo’s densely populated Al-Waraq neighbourhood in Imbaba district.
State media reported that the fire broke out when a truck loaded with fuel overturned on a crowded highway.
The health ministry said 39 ambulances were sent to the scene, and 15 people were taken to hospital with injuries.
Images from the site showed a grisly aftermath, with cars burnt out from the blaze apparently caused by the fuel truck overturning, as firefighters doused the truck’s wreckage.
Flames are seen in the Al-Waraq neighbourhood of Imbaba district in Cairo, Egypt, on Wednesday. Photo: UGC via AFP
A crowd and emergency services gathered at the scene as a bulldozer removed a car’s burnt-out wreckage, images showed.
Egypt, with its informal residential areas and often dilapidated infrastructure, has suffered several deadly fires in recent years.
Slow response times of emergency services are not unusual in the country, where neighbourhood residents routinely improvise rescue efforts, even within the megalopolis of Cairo.
Fire escapes, smoke detectors and alarms are rare and in many areas, warrens of narrow roads make it hard for fire engines to reach disaster sites.
Car crashes are also common, and often blamed on reckless driving, poor maintenance and uneven law enforcement, with traffic laws also being widely flouted.
Last year, nearly 6,000 people died in road accidents across the country, according to Egypt’s state statistics agency.
The year before, more than 5,200 road deaths were recorded across the country.
In August, at least 18 people, many of them teenagers, were killed in northern Egypt when two pickup trucks carrying agricultural day-labourers crashed.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: US finds no evidence China told Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, report says
content_en:
US officials say Alice Huang contacted China’s spy agency during the affair but found ⁠no indication ⁠she provided significant intelligence.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks with Alice Huang in Taipei, Taiwan, in June 2024. Photo: Reuters
US ⁠officials found no evidence ⁠that tech executive Alice Huang was directed by Beijing to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with a classified briefing.
The briefing ‌comes after US President Donald Trump cleared the way for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement earlier this week, assuring Nvidia that its CEO posed no national-security threat.
The controversy began with concerns over Alice Huang’s alleged Chinese intelligence links and whether her relationship with Jensen Huang affected suspected diversions ⁠of Nvidia chips to China.
Officials from the CIA, FBI, Office of the Director ‌of National Intelligence and National Security Agency briefed staff from congressional intelligence committees and chamber leaders, the Journal reported.
The officials said ‌Alice Huang contacted China’s spy agency during the affair but found ⁠no indication ⁠that she provided significant intelligence, the Journal reported.
[embedded media]
Nvidia and the agencies did not immediately respond ‌to a request for comment. Reuters could not independently verify the report.
Shares of Nvidia tumbled more ‌than 7 per cent, ‌putting the chipmaker on track to shed more than US$250 billion in ‌market value and eroding a 31 per cent comeback rally after CEO Huang’s reinstatement that ⁠added over US$900 billion.
The report said current evidence suggests that Alice Huang and Jensen ⁠Huang may have had an amorous relationship, but not a coordinated play by China, adding that new information could, however, change that ‌assessment.
The briefing also noted ‌that Kang Wei, described to the Journal as Alice Huang’s husband by people who know them, was an asset for China’s Ministry of State Security who remained in frequent contact with the intelligence service.
By Reuters
